verses.text: Now Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses, and for Israel his people, how that Yahweh had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, received Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her away,
and her two sons. The name of one son was Gershom,  for Moses said, “I have lived as a foreigner in a foreign land”.
The name of the other was Eliezer,  for he said, “My father’s God was my help and delivered me from Pharaoh’s sword.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses into the wilderness where he was encamped, at the Mountain of God.
He said to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, have come to you with your wife, and her two sons with her.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, and bowed and kissed him. They asked each other of their welfare, and they came into the tent.
Moses told his father-in-law all that Yahweh had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships that had come on them on the way, and how Yahweh delivered them.
Jethro rejoiced for all the goodness which Yahweh had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.
Jethro said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh; who has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.
Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all gods because of the thing in which they dealt arrogantly against them.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took a burnt offering and sacrifices for God. Aaron came with all the elders of Israel, to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God.
On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.
When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I make them know the statutes of God, and his laws.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”
So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.
Moses chose able men out of all Israel, and made them heads over the people, rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
They judged the people at all times. They brought the hard causes to Moses, but every small matter they judged themselves.
Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went his way into his own land.

footnotes.content: News travels in mysterious ways. Jethro heard from across the wilderness what the Lord had done for Moses and Israel—deliverance from Pharaoh himself. Sometimes the Lord's work speaks louder than our own voice can carry. The kindness is that Jethro cared enough to listen and come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zipporah, Moses' wife, was received back after being sent away—a quiet reunion in the shadow of history's great turning. Sometimes the smallest reunions matter as much as the grandest deliverances. The Lord mends the near before He mends the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gershom means "a foreigner there"—Moses named his own displacement, his belonging nowhere yet. Then, for years, the Lord used that very homelessness to shape a man who could lead a homeless people toward their home. Our sorrows often teach what our comfort could not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliezer: "God is my help." Named by a man who had fled Pharaoh's sword with his life, Moses gave his second son a name that speaks witness—the Lord saved us. A name is a prayer: this boy would grow up knowing his father trusted that salvation was real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro came to the wilderness, to the Mountain of God itself. He wasn't forced; he came to see. When faith begins to stir in the human heart, there's a desire to draw near, to witness the Lord for ourselves. Jethro's journey to the mountain was the beginning of his own conversion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to Jethro's courtesy: "I, your father-in-law Jethro, have come." He speaks with such humility, such care for the protocol between himself and Moses. Wisdom often wears gentleness; the counselor who respects his hearer will be heard when the brash fall silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses went out to meet him, bowed, and kissed him. There it was—the man who stood before Pharaoh, who parted the sea, showed honor to his elder with his whole body. Strength does not diminish respect; it makes respect deeper and more real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses told it all: every hardship, every redemption. The witness of the Lord's work begs to be spoken aloud. There's something about naming our trials and the Lord's faithfulness together—it makes both real. Jethro needed to hear the whole story to believe the whole God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro rejoiced. This is the heart of conversion: genuine joy at what God has done for others, even those not yet known to him. The goodness of the Lord is so immense that strangers can hear of it and be glad. Rejoicing in the deliverance of others is the first gate to faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro blessed the Lord—not as a foreigner now, but as one who recognized the God of Israel. "Blessed be Yahweh" came from a Midianite priest's lips. The Lord's name crossed a boundary that morning. When the Lord moves, every mountain people hears the echo.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all gods." Jethro's confession is a tiny seed of the truth that would one day spread across all nations. He saw the Lord's power against the gods of Egypt and believed. The knowledge of God grows in us when we witness His triumph over what we once feared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro brought burnt offerings and sacrifices; Aaron and the elders came to eat before God. This meal, this worship together—it was the seal of covenant, the ancient way of saying: we are one people before the Lord now. Communion at the foot of Sinai began with a foreigner's open heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the next day, Moses sat to judge from morning to evening. The people stood—a whole nation waiting for wisdom, for justice, for the Lord's will to be known. Moses bore that weight entirely on his shoulders, though he did not yet see it as too much to bear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro watched and saw something amiss: "What is this thing?" Sometimes an outsider sees what the one in the midst cannot see. Moses was burning out; the work was impossible. Love sometimes wears the face of an honest question from someone who loves you enough to speak it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses answered simply: the people come to inquire of God, so he judges between them. He spoke the truth of what he was doing—but didn't yet hear the question underneath Jethro's words: You cannot do this alone, and you were never meant to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When disputes arose, Moses taught God's statutes and laws. He was not just a judge; he was a teacher, an intermediary between heaven and earth. But the weight of it—every matter, every day—began to crush him. Even sacred work must be shared or it becomes a burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jethro spoke directly: "The thing you do is not good." How merciful this elder was, to be so honest. Sometimes the people we love most see what will destroy us before we do. Jethro's hard word was an act of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You will surely wear away, both you and the people." Not one would perish from Jethro's warning, but both would suffer if the burden remained unsplit. The Lord does not call anyone to burn out alone. We are designed for community, for shared labor, for help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Listen to my voice," Jethro urged gently. Then he held up the truth: Moses was to stand for the people before God, to bring their causes to Him. But that didn't mean Moses had to do everything—just the things only he could do. Delegation is not abandonment; it is wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses' chief work was teaching—showing the people the way they must walk and the work they must do. A leader's highest calling is not to do all the work, but to teach others how to do it. The Lord multiplies our labor through faithful teaching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Able men who fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain." Jethro named the character of leaders—not the brilliant or the powerful, but those who fear the Lord and despise corruption. These criteria, spoken beside Sinai, echo still. The Lord looks for faithful hearts, not impressive résumés.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves." The wisdom here is profound: not all problems require the chief, and to believe otherwise exhausts everyone. Knowing what needs your hand and what can be released is the mark of a wise leader.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If you will do this, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure." Jethro's condition was not doubt but hope—if Moses listens and God affirms, then both Moses and the people will go to their place in peace. Organization rooted in God's will brings rest, not just efficiency.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses listened. This man who spoke to God face to face, who worked wonders, heard his father-in-law and received his counsel as good. Humility is not weakness but wisdom: to hear, to consider, to obey when advice is sound. Moses became greater, not smaller, by listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses chose able men and set them over the people in descending tiers—thousands, hundreds, fifties, tens. The whole structure arose from one act of obedience. When we share work according to capacity, we build something that stands. Delegation done rightly is multiplication.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They judged the people at all times." The system worked. Justice remained steady; the people were served; the hard cases still reached Moses. Boundaries and delegation did not diminish the work—they made it sustainable. The Lord was pleased with this ordering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this farewell: Jethro returned to his land, but he had given Moses a gift that endured—the gift of wise counsel received with humility, of systems that blessed generations. We rarely know which wise elder's word will reshape history. As of 2026-10, we are grateful for those who speak hard truth in love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
